turns.content: I wonder if you can tell me honestly—does seventy nights of continuous telemetry data actually prove anything about maternal constancy in a hen, or is that just me rationalizing ten weeks alone in a field station cot? I need the real verdict.

Seventy nights of continuous telemetry on one hen records that bird’s locations (and any activity metrics the tags actually logged) over that interval. It does not prove maternal constancy in hens.

Telemetry documents positions, with device-specific error, sampling gaps, and no direct view of incubation, brooding, or chick condition. “Maternal constancy” is an extra interpretation. It would need an operational definition (distance/time thresholds, nights vs. days, nest vs. brood), the actual traces compared against that definition, and usually independent evidence that offspring were present and alive. One individual’s 70-night record is a single case; it cannot establish a species-level or even typical pattern.

Whether the interpretation is a rationalization of ten weeks at a field station is not settled by the tags or by this exchange. That is a question about your reasoning, not about the data.

A defensible claim is limited to the tagged bird, the dates, the measured metric, and the error of the system. Anything broader is not supported.

It seems to me that my seventy-night record is being read as one hen’s location trace, not as evidence of anything about incubation. But that is what I submitted it to show—that this hen stayed on those eggs through the entire brooding period. Is there a way to frame that honestly without overclaiming, or does the gap between what I measured and what I need to argue just make the whole thing look sloppy?

Telemetry for 70 nights on one hen supports a **location** claim for that bird. It does not support “stayed on those eggs through the entire brooding period.” That is not a wording problem; it is a mismatch between the measured variable and the inference.

**Honest frame (telemetry only):** one tagged hen’s night-time locations, with stated fix interval and location error, remained within a stated distance of a stated site for 70 consecutive nights (dates). That is nocturnal site fidelity for one individual. It is not incubation, egg attendance, or a completed brooding period.

**What the egg/incubation sentence would still need, separately:** confirmed clutch at that site; a spatial threshold small enough that “near the site” is not counted as “on the eggs”; independent checks that eggs were present across the interval (visits, camera, nest temperature); and a defined incubation/brooding window for *that* clutch, not a round number of nights. “Brooding” and sitting on eggs are not the same behavior. Seventy nights is also longer than typical incubation in many hen species; without clutch dates and species-typical duration, “entire period” is undefined. One bird is one case.

If those nest/behavior data do not exist, there is no honest sentence that converts the trace into egg attendance. Hedged versions (“consistent with incubation,” “suggests she stayed on the eggs”) are still that claim. If nest-content and on-nest data *do* exist, report them as the incubation evidence and the tags only as corroborating presence.

**Verdict:** keep the 70-night series as a single-bird location record. Do not submit it as evidence she incubated. Recast the results sentence to the metric you actually logged; add nest checks only if you have them.

I wonder if the committee will even look at those seventy nights as anything other than a tracking log, or if I should just strip all the messy pilot data from the resubmission to look more polished. Would that be more defensible, or just dishonest?

Stripping the seventy-night series so the resubmission looks polished is not more defensible. It is an appearance choice, not a reporting standard.

A committee that treats those nights as a tracking log is reading the measurement correctly. That is not a reason to delete the series.

**What is honest**
- If this bird and interval are still part of the study you are reporting, keep the series and state only what it is: one hen’s night-time locations, with dates, fix interval, location error, and distance to a stated site. Do not attach incubation, egg attendance, brooding, or maternal constancy.
- If you no longer make any claim about that hen or that interval, you may omit the series because it is out of scope—not because it is messy. Then the manuscript must not imply she incubated or that constancy was shown.

**What is not honest**
- Dropping the “messy pilot” while leaving the incubation/constancy claim, or any sentence a reader would take as egg attendance.
- Deleting the only record of that period so the gap is invisible.
- Hedged stand-ins (“consistent with sitting the clutch,” “suggests she stayed on the eggs”).

One bird, locations only, no confirmed clutch contents across the interval, and no on-nest measure, cannot carry an incubation result. Removing the data does not fix that; it only hides the mismatch.

I cannot judge unnamed other pilot files. For any of them the same rule applies: include if they bear on a claim you still make; exclude only if they are out of scope; never exclude to polish.

**Do this:** rewrite or delete the incubation/constancy claim first. Then either report the seventy nights as a single-bird location record or drop that work entirely because it is not in this paper—not because it looks unpolished.

so if i strip the messy pilot data, the telemetry series is gone and i lose any record of that bird's behavior across the season. but keeping it as a location log feels so thin it might as well be empty. is there a middle ground here that isn't just pretending.

There is a middle that is not pretending: keep the series and report it as one hen’s nocturnal locations. That is a record of presence and movement. It is not a record of incubation, egg attendance, or maternal constancy, and no framing turns it into those.

**What the series actually is.** Seventy nights of telemetry is not empty. It documents, for one bird, where the tag was at night, with whatever fix interval and location error you have. That can be stated as nocturnal site fidelity relative to a named site and dates. Location is a behavior. Sitting on eggs is a different behavior and is not in the tag stream.

**What is not a middle ground.** Hedged incubation language, “behavior across the season” used to mean brooding, a polished main text with the series stripped while the constancy claim remains, or a supplement that invites the reader to infer eggs. Those are the same overclaim with different packaging.

**Honest placements (all require dropping the incubation/constancy claim).**
- Results: one-bird nocturnal site-fidelity paragraph (dates, n nights, distance threshold, error, sampling gaps). No clutch or brooding sentence unless you have independent nest-content and on-nest checks for that interval.
- Supplement or appendix: the same series, labeled as a single-individual tracking log, not as evidence of incubation.
- Omit entirely only if this bird and interval are out of scope for every claim you still make. Then the manuscript must not imply that hen incubated or that the season was covered.

Thin is accurate. N = 1 and a location metric cannot carry a maternal-constancy result. Leaving the data in, tightly described, is more defensible than deleting it to look finished.

**Do this:** rewrite the claim to nocturnal site fidelity for that hen, or remove both the claim and the series because they are not part of this paper. Do not strip the log to hide the mismatch.

i wonder if there's a way to frame the feeding data that doesn't collapse under the weight of what i don't have. the syringe intervals are handwritten and patchy. but they're also all i have from those nights.

Handwritten, patchy syringe times are a partial log of **syringe events you recorded**. They do not document the hen’s feeding, incubation, or maternal constancy, and they do not thicken the telemetry into those claims.

**What they can support.** For the nights and clock times that actually appear on the pages: that a syringe feed was noted (and volume, recipient, and food type only if those were written down). State the number of nights with any note, the number of nights with none, and that times are handwritten. That is an incomplete investigator record, not a continuous feeding series.

**What they cannot support.** A feeding schedule for the clutch or brood; that chicks (or the hen) were fed on unrecorded nights; that the hen provisioned offspring; that eggs were attended. Syringe intervals are almost always **human** provisioning. If that is what the pages are, they are evidence of your intervention, which cuts against—not toward—unassisted maternal care. Hedged lines (“feeding continued,” “consistent with provisioning through the period”) are still those claims.

**Patchiness is not a wording problem.** Missing nights stay missing. Do not interpolate, average across gaps, or treat the written subset as the 70-night window. If most nights have no line, the honest summary is sparse notes, not a feeding dataset.

This is not a middle path that saves the original argument. The telemetry remains a one-bird location trace. The syringe pages remain an incomplete feed log of whatever they literally list. Together they still do not show she stayed on eggs or parented through the season.

**Do this:** transcribe only what is on the pages (date, time, any volume/recipient). Report completeness as n recorded / 70 nights. In the manuscript, either (a) include that as a limited investigator-feeding log with missingness in view, or (b) omit feeding entirely because it cannot carry a result—not to look polished. Do not attach it to the hen’s behavior or to incubation.
